title: Echinacea infusion at cold onset
subtitle: A short acute infusion at the first sign of a cold
excerpt: A hot infusion of dried echinacea aerial parts, taken at the very first sign of a cold. This is the infusion preparation, distinct from the tincture (which is used for systemic immune support over a course). The infusion contacts the throat mucosa directly. One teaspoon of dried aerial parts per 200 ml, steeped covered for ten minutes, for five to seven days maximum.
sourceNotes: Felter and Lloyd, King's American Dispensatory (1898), echinacea entry: the primary Eclectic-American reference documenting echinacea for acute infections at onset, and the short-course acute use pattern. Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), echinacea entry. EMA HMPC monograph on Echinaceae purpureae herba (2015): documents traditional acute use, allergen note for Asteraceae, autoimmune caution.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dried echinacea aerial parts store 12 months in a sealed tin away from light. Prepare each cup fresh.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Prepare fresh for each dose. Do not store the brewed infusion.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preparation made by pouring just-boiled water over leaves or flowers and steeping them covered, so the volatile oils stay in the cup rather than escaping with the steam.
The above-ground portions of the plant: stems, leaves, and flowers. In echinacea, the aerial parts are used separately from the root, and carry the active compounds in a different ratio.

content.text: Echinacea infusion is a hot cup of dried echinacea aerial parts in just-boiled water. Taken at the very first sign of a cold. This is the acute infusion preparation, quite different from an echinacea alcohol extract taken over a longer course for systemic immune help: the hot infusion contacts the mucous membranes of the throat directly, which is the traditional starting point for an acute cold response. One teaspoon of dried aerial parts per 200 ml, steeped covered for ten minutes. it is a short-course remedy of five to seven days only.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. Allergen note: echinacea belongs to the daisy family (Asteraceae). Readers with a known allergy to ragweed, daisies, chamomile, or related plants should not use this preparation without first consulting a herbalist or doctor. Autoimmune conditions: traditional western herbal practice avoids long-term echinacea use in readers with autoimmune conditions including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis. This is because the herb modulates immune activity. For an acute short course at cold onset this is less of a concern. But readers with an autoimmune condition should still consult their herbalist or GP before use. Course length: this is a short acute remedy only. Do not take echinacea infusion continuously for more than seven days without a break. Prolonged continuous use is outside the traditional use pattern and is not appropriate for self-care. Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine, or a paediatric doctor, before using any herbal preparation in children under twelve.

content.text: Put 1 teaspoon of dried echinacea aerial parts into a teapot or covered cup.
Pour over 200 ml of just-boiled water and lid immediately.

Steep covered for 10 minutes. The water turns a pale golden-brown and smells lightly herbal. Fresh echinacea tea typically produces a mild tingling sensation at the back of the throat, which is normal.
Strain through a sieve and drink warm.

attrs.title: The tingling sensation
attrs.body: A mild tingling or numbing at the back of the throat is normal with good-quality dried echinacea. It is caused by the alkylamide compounds in the herb. If you feel no tingling at all, the dried herb may have lost potency through age or poor storage.

content.text: One cup (200 ml) up to three times a day, at the first sign of symptoms. For a short acute course of five to seven days only. Do not take continuously beyond seven days. If symptoms worsen, a fever develops, or you are not improving after five days, see your doctor.
Prepare each cup fresh. Dried echinacea aerial parts store in a sealed tin or jar, away from light and heat, for up to 12 months.
When not to use this remedy
See a doctor if symptoms last more than ten days, fever rises above 39°C, breathing is laboured, or symptoms worsen after at first improving.

Do not use if you have a known Asteraceae allergy. Readers with an autoimmune condition should consult their herbalist or GP before use. Do not use in children under twelve without specialist guidance. Do not take for more than seven days without a break.

items.symptom: No tingling sensation and very faint flavour
items.cause: Dried echinacea has lost potency through age or poor storage
items.fix: Replace with fresh dried echinacea aerial parts. A mild throat tingle is the quality marker for active echinacea.
